2027-05-10.title: Mar Shemun Shleeha the Zealot · St Simon the Apostle · Monday of the sixth week after Qyomtho
readings: Paul stays in Ephesus until Pentecost: a wide door for effective work has opened
Zacchaeus: today salvation has come to this house
2027-05-10.alt: Season of Qyomtho (the Resurrection): the ten days of waiting between Suloko (the Ascension) and Pentecost, in the week after the Sixth Sunday after Qyomtho. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Shemun Shleeha the Zealot, St Simon the Apostle.
2027-05-10.verse: For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.
theo: Four days after Suloko, the Church is in the upper room. The Lord has gone up to the Father, the Spirit has not yet come, and the Panchangam reminds us that in these ten days no wedding celebrations are held: the whole Church holds its breath and prays. It is fitting that today we remember one of the men who sat in that very room. St Luke gives the list of those who waited: “Peter, and John, and James, and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, and Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James.” This is Mar Shemun Shleeha, whom our Church calls “the zealous one.” St Matthew and St Mark call him “the Cananaean,” from an Aramaic word for zeal; St Luke translates it as “the Zealot.” Whether Simon had belonged to the party of armed patriots who longed to drive out the Romans, or whether the name simply marked a man burning with zeal for God's Law, the Gospels do not say, and scholars still discuss it. What happened to him after Pentecost is told differently by different Churches: some ancient traditions send him with St Jude to preach in Persia and to die there as a martyr; others speak of Egypt or other lands. We hold to what is sure: Jesus chose him, Jesus changed the direction of his zeal, and on the day of Pentecost he was among those on whom the fire came down.

The Gospel shows us why such a man could follow Jesus. In Jericho there lived Zacchaeus, “a chief tax collector” who “was rich.” Tax collectors worked for the occupying power and often took more than was due; a zealot would have counted him a traitor to his people. Yet Zacchaeus, short in stature and long in curiosity, “ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see him.” Jesus stopped beneath the tree: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.” The crowd grumbled, “He has gone to be the guest of one who is a sinner.” But grace had already done its work. Zacchaeus stood and said, “Look, half of my possessions, Lord, I will give to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I will pay back four times as much.” Then came the great word: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.” Think of the company of the Twelve: Simon the Zealot and Matthew the tax collector sat at the same table and ate the same bread. Only Jesus could make brothers of such men. St Augustine says that Zacchaeus climbed the sycamore as we must climb the Cross: the humble wood that seems foolish to the proud is the place from which we see the Lord passing by (Sermon 174, in substance). Simon's zeal did not die when he met Jesus; it was turned from hatred of the sinner to love of the lost.

St Paul's words to the Corinthians come from the same season of the year. “I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,” he writes, “for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.” Paul counted the days towards Pentecost, as we do now. He saw a door open, and he saw opposition too, and he did not run from either. Then he speaks with tenderness of his younger helper: “If Timothy comes, see that he has nothing to fear among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord just as I am; therefore let no one despise him.” And of Apollos, who would not come just then: “He will come when he has the opportunity.” Here is zeal that has learned patience and gentleness. It does not crush the young or force the reluctant; it waits for God's time. That is the lesson of these ten days. The apostles did not rush out of the upper room on the day after the Ascension to begin their own campaign. They waited, “constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus.” Holy zeal begins on its knees. Then the Spirit opens the wide door.
conn: The Zealot in the upper room.
Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13: Simon is named among the Twelve and among those who waited in prayer with Mary for the Holy Spirit.
Psalm 69:9, quoted in John 2:17: the zeal that consumed Jesus is the zeal he gives to his apostles, a zeal for God and for the lost.
Luke 19:10 echoes Ezekiel 34:16, where God promises to seek the lost himself; in Jesus the Shepherd of Israel walks into Jericho.
fathers: Zacchaeus was small and climbed a tree to see Jesus; let us also climb the tree of the Cross, which the proud mock, so that we may see the Lord who passes by (Sermon 174, in substance).
Let the rich learn that the fault lies not in possessions themselves but in those who do not know how to use them; Zacchaeus became great by giving (Exposition of the Gospel of Luke 8, in substance).
magis: Jesus is the Father's Emissary. From the beginning of his ministry, he called to him those whom he desired, and appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, to be with him and to be sent out to preach.

The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his spiritual and bodily necessities; giving alms to the poor is one of the chief witnesses to fraternal charity.

The Lord Jesus, after praying to the Father, called to himself those whom he desired and appointed twelve to be with him; he formed them after the manner of a college, and sent them to proclaim the Kingdom of God (in substance).
outline: Ask: what am I zealous about, and does my zeal look like Jesus?
A burning heart chosen and turned towards the Kingdom.
Zacchaeus, the tax collector, found by the Lord who seeks the lost.
Point 3 · A wide door at Pentecost
Zeal that waits, prays and is gentle with others.
“For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.”
live: Think of one person you have written off as beyond change. Pray for that person by name every day until Pentecost.
Let no one despise him (1 Corinthians 16:11)
Find one young person in your parish or family who is doing the Lord's work, and give a word of encouragement this week.
2027-05-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came to seek out and to save the lost, and you stopped beneath the sycamore tree to call Zacchaeus by name. You chose Mar Shemun the Zealot and turned the fire of his heart towards your Kingdom. In these days of waiting between your Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit, gather us with your apostles and with your holy Mother in prayer. Purify our zeal from anger and pride, make it patient and gentle, and open for us the wide door of your work. By the prayers of Mar Shemun Shleeha, let salvation come to our homes today, and make us glad to welcome you. To you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: Zacchaeus received Jesus into his house and was changed; at the Holy Qurbono the Lord says to each of us again, “I must stay at your house today,” and comes to us in his Body and Blood.

quick: St Simon the Zealot, one of the Twelve, waited in the upper room with Mary for the Spirit; Jesus turned his zeal towards the Kingdom.
Zacchaeus the tax collector climbed a tree to see Jesus; Jesus called him by name and salvation came to his house.
Paul stayed in Ephesus until Pentecost because a wide door had opened; holy zeal is patient, prayerful and gentle.
2027-05-10.action: Pray by name for one person you have given up on, and ask Jesus to stop at that person's house.
2027-05-10.question: Is my zeal for God turned against people, or towards the lost?
term: The Syriac word for apostle, meaning one who is sent. Our Church gives this title to the Twelve, to St Paul, and to those whom tradition counts among the first preachers, such as Mar Shemun Shleeha and Mar Addai Shleeha.
kidsaint: St Simon, the apostle with a fiery heart

Simon was called “the Zealot,” which means he was full of zeal, a burning love for God. Before he met Jesus, he may have wanted to fight the Romans. Jesus taught him a better way: to love even people he did not like, like Matthew, who had been a tax collector. Simon learned to put his fire into telling everyone about Jesus. Lesson: when you feel strongly about something, ask Jesus to turn that strong feeling into love.

family.explain: Zacchaeus was a short man who climbed a tree to see Jesus. Everyone thought he was a bad man, but Jesus called him by name and went to his house. Zacchaeus was so happy that he gave half of what he had to the poor and paid back everyone he had cheated.
family.intention: We pray for someone who seems far from God, that Jesus may visit that person's home.
family.ask: Ask: “If Jesus said today, ‘I must stay at your house,’ what would we want to put right first?”

illus: In a town near Adoor there was a man the neighbours called “the moneylender.” His interest was high and his heart seemed hard. A young parish priest, new to the town, began to stop at his gate every evening on the way back from the house blessings, only to greet him and ask after his health. For months the man answered with a grunt. Then one evening, during the days before Pentecost, he invited the priest in. “Everyone else crosses the road when they see me,” he said. “Why do you stop?” The priest answered, “Because Jesus stopped under a tree in Jericho.” Within a year the old man had cancelled the debts of two widows and was coming to the Holy Qurbono on Sundays. No sermon had changed him. A man who kept stopping at his gate had.

pm.open: Christ is risen! Lord Jesus, you came to seek the lost. As we wait for your Holy Spirit, stop at our house today and call each of us by name. Amen.
share: Simon, who was called the Zealot (Luke 6:15). What am I zealous about, and how could Jesus turn that zeal towards his Kingdom?
Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today (Luke 19:5). Where in my life is Jesus asking me to come down quickly?
A wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries (1 Corinthians 16:9). What door is God opening for our prayer group?
interc: For the Church in these days before Pentecost, that like the apostles we may wait in prayer with Mary for the Holy Spirit.
For those who have strayed from the faith and those whom others have given up on, that the Lord may find them.
For tax officials, business people and all who handle money, that they may be honest and generous to the poor.
For young people who serve in our parish, that no one may despise them and that they may grow in courage.
For the Churches that honour St Simon, that his prayers may keep them zealous for the Gospel.
pm.close: Lord Jesus, you made the Zealot and the tax collector brothers at your table. Make our zeal gentle and our hearts open, and send your Spirit upon us. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Christ is risen! We are living in the ten days between Suloko and Pentecost. The apostles are in the upper room, waiting and praying, and today our Church remembers one of them: Mar Shemun Shleeha, St Simon the Zealot. We know little about his life, but his name tells us something important. He was a man of zeal, a man with fire in his heart. Before he met Jesus, that fire may have burned against the Romans and against anyone who served them. After he met Jesus, it burned for the Kingdom of God.

In the Gospel we meet the very kind of man a zealot would have despised: Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, rich from other people's money. The crowd blocked his way, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree. And Jesus stopped. He looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today.” Notice: Jesus did not wait for Zacchaeus to become good before he came to his house. He came first, and his coming made Zacchaeus good. The man who had taken now began to give: half of his possessions to the poor, and four times back to anyone he had cheated.

Now picture the table of the Twelve. Simon the Zealot on one side, Matthew the former tax collector on the other. In the world they would have been enemies. At the table of Jesus they were brothers. This is what the Holy Spirit will do at Pentecost: not take away our zeal, but purify it. The anger goes; the fire stays. St Paul, waiting in Ephesus “until Pentecost,” shows us what purified zeal looks like. He sees a wide door and many adversaries, and he is not afraid. He tells the Corinthians to protect young Timothy and to let Apollos come in his own time. That is zeal with patience, zeal with gentleness.

So in these days of waiting, let us ask ourselves: is there a Zacchaeus in my life, someone I have written off? Let us pray for that person by name until Pentecost. And let us let Jesus say to us too, “I must stay at your house today.” He will say it at this altar, when he comes to us in his Body and Blood. Let us hurry down and welcome him with joy.
kids: Children, Christ is risen! Have you ever climbed a tree to see something far away? In today's Gospel a short man named Zacchaeus climbed a tree to see Jesus, because the crowd was too big. Nobody liked Zacchaeus, because he took too much money from people. But Jesus stopped right under the tree, looked up and called him by his name! Jesus went to his house, and Zacchaeus was so happy that he decided to give money to the poor and pay back everyone he had cheated. Today we also remember St Simon, one of Jesus' twelve friends. He had a fiery heart, and Jesus taught him to use that fire for love. This week, be kind to someone others leave out. That is what Jesus did.

intro: Theme: “For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.”
On the memory of Mar Shemun Shleeha the Zealot, in the days of waiting before Pentecost: the apostle with a fiery heart, the tax collector found by grace, and zeal that waits for the Spirit.

points.h: Simon the Zealot: a fire chosen by Christ
sub: Waiting in the upper room with Mary.
Zeal turned from anger to love.
q: It is zeal for your house that has consumed me; the insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.
Do not lag in zeal, be ardent in spirit, serve the Lord.
points.apply: Name the thing you are most zealous about and offer it to Jesus in prayer each morning until Pentecost.

sub: A short man in a sycamore tree.
Half to the poor, fourfold to the wronged.
q: I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed
The saying is sure and worthy of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners

sub: Paul counts the days to Pentecost.
Zeal that begins on its knees.
q: Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!
All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus, as well as his brothers.

concl: Jesus chose a zealot and a tax collector and made them brothers; the Spirit purifies our zeal without putting out its fire.
In these ten days the Church waits on its knees, and the Lord stops at every house that longs to see him.
2027-05-10.resolve: Pray for one person you had given up on, put right one wrong, and wait for the Spirit in prayer with Mary.
